To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a new approach for Raman spectroscopy enhancement by entrapping analytes into charge-transfer complexes, immobilized onto nanostructures.

the entrapping of the analyte into the CT complex immobilized on the surface of the nanostructured substrate is a key factor for the Raman enhancement, which can be used to expand the range of the analytes that can be detected by the Raman technique.

(a) Raman scattering enhancement is achieved by entrapping analyte molecules into charge-transfer complexes formed between a dye and an electron donor, and immobilizing these complexes onto nanostructured substrata; (b) the enhancement mechanism relies on a combination of the resonance effect, the surface enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) effect, and the effect of a charge-transfer complex on the analyte's Raman spectrum.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel approach for Raman enhancement by immobilization of analyte in charge-transfer complexes on nanostructured substrates, which are able to trap analytes in a confined space and to enhance their Raman scattering.
the development of new materials for resonant RRS enhancement of analytes.
the development of novel nanostructured surfaces that are able to enhance the Raman scattering of analytes that can form charge-transfer complexes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Raman scattering enhancement observed in this communication is due to a charge-transfer interaction between the analyte and the immobilized charge-transfer complex.
the charge-transfer complex of the analyte with the acceptor is the key factor to be considered in the design of the substrate for the enhancement of Raman scattering of the analyte.

the present study has shown that the use of a nanostructured substrate for the immobilization of a charge-transfer complex has allowed to obtain an enhancement of the Raman scattering intensity for a wide range of analytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Raman enhancement is achieved by the formation of charge-transfer complexes between the analyte and the substrate and the enhancement is proportional to the amount of charge-transfer complexes formed.
the combination of charge-transfer complexes and nanostructured substrates provides a new platform for the Raman scattering enhancement of a broad range of analytes.
we can now use the same nanostructured substrate to enhance Raman scattering for analytes of different chemical nature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of charge-transfer complexes for Raman scattering can expand the range of important molecules becoming available for resonant enhancement.
the Raman enhancement of the charge-transfer complexes is a consequence of the formation of the complex, which in turn is due to the strong electronic coupling between the analytes and the substrate.

a variety of organic compounds, including those of pharmaceutical interest, can be trapped into charge-transfer complexes with a suitable donor molecule, immobilized onto nanostructures, and used for resonant RRS enhancement.
